Charles Leclerc’s radio transcript disproves his claim about Lewis Hamilton controversy at Dutch GP

David Comerford
Mon 24 August 2026 12:00, UK
Follow us on Google Discover
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:28
Instaread

Ferrari have faced criticism for choosing not to impose team orders to help Lewis Hamilton during Sunday’s Dutch Grand Prix.

Hamilton dropped behind Leclerc on the opening lap of the race but ran longer in his first stint, which gave him a powerful tyre offset in the second. When he caught up to his teammate, he complained that he was losing valuable time.

However, Ferrari did not order Leclerc to move aside and Hamilton only enjoyed the benefit of clean air when his teammate pitted after spending multiple laps on his gearbox.

Where do you stand on Ferrari’s lack of team orders at the Dutch GP?

Lewis Hamilton was fuming that they didn't tell Charles Leclerc to let him past

Charles Leclerc didn’t follow Ferrari instruction to box

At one stage, Leclerc appeared to ignore an instruction to pit, which would have released Hamilton earlier. After the race, he claimed in an interview with Canal Plus that he had been asked to stay out.

“The team first asked me, at the beginning of the lap, to come in to the pits, but at the end of the lap, they asked me to stay out on track,” he explained. “So that’s what I did. And I think two laps later, I finally came in to the pits.”

However, The Race have studied Leclerc’s radio transcript and found no evidence that the call to box was cancelled. In fact, after querying the strategy, which gave him a minimal offset compared to George Russell, he was expressly reminded to come in.

Engineer Bryan Bozzi: “Box, Charles, box.”

Leclerc: “What do you mean box-box? Why stop two laps after Russell? [25-second silence] Hello?”

More F1 Stories

Bozzi: “Yep coming back to you. [Pause] Charles, we want to box.”

For whatever reason, Leclerc didn’t pit until a lap later, and after the race, Hamilton said Ferrari cost themselves a podium by mismanaging the situation. He crossed the line just eight-tenths of a second behind Russell.

  • READ MORE: Charles Leclerc’s gesture at Lewis Hamilton says it all after Ferrari near-miss at Dutch Grand Prix

Ferrari didn’t tell Hamilton at the time because they wanted to keep their cards close to their chest, but the plan was for the Briton to one-stop. This only changed when Esteban Ocon’s stoppage led to a virtual safety car.

They knew Leclerc, on a different strategy, was due in imminently, but he held up the sister car for a lap longer than anticipated.
